## My Thinking

I have 10 mu of contracted land, same as always. My family depends on it, so I won't take risks. Every farmer around here does winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same plots — that's what I do too. My neighbor Liu's family tried switching to peanuts two years ago and had trouble selling them. I'll stick with what I know.

For wheat, I'll plant the Jimai variety — the village seed station sells it and the county extension people promoted it last spring. I don't fully trust the newer hybrids the salesman pushed at the market; too expensive, too unfamiliar. For maize I always use Zhengdan 958 hybrid, everyone uses it and it does well here.

Water is the hard part. We're on deep well irrigation and the water table has been dropping. My husband and I can afford about 3 pump sessions for wheat and 2 for maize if the summer rains are weak. That's what we've done for years.

For fertilizer, I apply di-ammonium phosphate and urea, same as my father-in-law taught me. The amounts I use are what I was shown — I don't measure precisely, but I can estimate in bags. I apply a bit more nitrogen on wheat because the heads need it.

After wheat harvest in June, I seed the maize directly into the stubble with the village's shared seeder — no need to plow again. Saves money and time.

Fertilizer rates follow what I learned from my father-in-law and what the extension station has told us over the years — heavier nitrogen on wheat for grain fill, lighter on maize. I irrigate wheat three times at key stages and maize twice given summer rainfall uncertainty, always mindful of the well costs and falling groundwater. After wheat harvest I plant maize directly into the stubble to save labor and fuel. I apply pesticides for wheat aphids and powdery mildew and for maize stem borers. I do not experiment with new crops or practices because the price risk is too high for a household that depends entirely on this land."
